**Paragraph 1 — Identity & Significance**

Gaius Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus was a Roman Christian poet from Hispania, specifically from the city of Cordoba, whose works were widely recognized in the early Christian era.

He is best known for his epic poem 'Ecclesiastica', which tells the story of the early Christian church and its struggles, and is considered one of the most important Christian poets of the 4th century.

Juvencus' poetry played a significant role in shaping the Christian liturgy and liturgical language, and his influence can be seen in the works of later Christian poets and scholars.

**Paragraph 2 — What Happened**

Juvencus' life and work are shrouded in mystery, but it is known that he was born in Hispania and traveled extensively throughout the Roman Empire, visiting places such as Rome, Jerusalem, and Antioch.

He is believed to have written his poetry in the 380s CE, during the reign of Emperor Theodosius I, and it is thought that he may have been influenced by the Christianization of the Roman Empire under Theodosius.

Juvencus' poetry was well-received by his contemporaries, and he was praised by his fellow poet, St. Ambrose, for his skill and artistry.

**Paragraph 3 — Legacy & Consequence**

Juvencus' poetry had a lasting impact on the development of Christian liturgy and liturgical language, and his works were widely studied and imitated by later Christian scholars and poets.

His influence can be seen in the works of later Christian poets, such as St. Augustine and St. Gregory the Great, and his poetry continues to be studied and admired by scholars and readers today.

Juvencus' legacy is also reflected in the many translations and adaptations of his poetry that have been made over the centuries, and his works remain an important part of the Christian literary canon.
